When assessing the capacity of women’s shelters to accommodate women and their children, the standards provided by Article 23 of the Istanbul Convention were applied. For this methodology, one family shelter place is considered to be equivalent to one shelter bed space. When referring to family places, the Istanbul Convention and its Explanatory Report set a minimum requirement of one family place (covering two beds, one for a woman and one for a child) per 10,000 population.<sup>45</sup> This standard is a valuable tool for assessing the availability of beds in shelters accessible to women and for comparing data across countries, and it is applied in the related chapter and in the tables. Nevertheless, as the specific needs of each country may vary, as acknowledged in the Istanbul Convention Explanatory Report,<sup>46</sup> compliance with this standard is not included in the country profiles; rather, it is used to assess its availability at the European level.

Similarly, the availability of an adequate number of beds in a specific country does not necessarily reflect the accessibility of shelters for different groups of survivors. Therefore, respondents were asked if the shelters in their country are accessible to the following groups of survivors: women with uncertain residence status, undocumented women, refugee women, homeless women, women with physical, cognitive or sensory disabilities, women with substance abuse issues, older women, transgender women, women with older sons, women with children with disabilities and unaccompanied girls under the age of 18. Additionally, it was assessed if there are any shelters specialised in supporting particular groups, e.g., migrant/undocumented women, women with disabilities, Black and minority ethnic women, LGBTQI+ people, older women, or women survivors of specific forms of violence such as trafficking, ‘honour-based’ violence, forced marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM). This information, wherever available, is included in the country profiles in order to provide a clearer picture of the accessibility of shelter services in Europe.

The definition of women’s centres includes all women’s services providing non-residential specialist support to survivors and can encompass a broad range of women’s centres. Many women’s centres focus on counselling; however, WAVE recognises that not all women’s centres necessarily provide these services, e.g., some focus primarily or solely on prevention work and advocacy. The relevant tables of the Report include the proportion of the female population per centre, and highlight that in most cases, there are not enough centres to comply with the Council of Europe recommendation of one counselling centre for VAW survivors for every 50,000 women. Secondly, the tables relating to women’s centres indicate who the beneficiaries of such centres are, as in some cases they are women-only, in other cases they support all survivors of GBV; finally, the tables include a column to show whether centres are run by women’s NGOs, other NGOs,

the State, or other providers. This information is relevant because it indicates the general approach to service provision in each country. WAVE recognises that women’s NGOs mostly have a gendered understanding and analysis of VAW, and that their service provision is based on a feminist, gender-sensitive approach that aims to empower women.

Section: Research preparation > Countries included in the data collection > Methodological approach to collect and assess data

As in the shelters section, additional accessibility information was gathered regarding women’s centres. Whenever available, the country profiles provide information on specialist support for particular groups of survivors and women survivors at risk of specific forms of violence. Article 25 of the Istanbul Convention makes specific reference to the provision of support for survivors of sexualised violence. The requirements are that states provide for the establishment of “appropriate, easily accessible rape crisis or sexual violence referral centres” for survivors, with the recommendation being one centre available for every 200,000 inhabitants. Therefore, data on the availability of women’s centres and support services for survivors of sexualised violence are presented in different sections of the Country Report. Although sexualised violence can also be a form of domestic violence, specialised services for survivors of sexualised violence should be analysed separately from domestic violence services. Importantly, sexualised violence can be committed irrespective of the relationship between the perpetrator and the survivor, in any setting, including but not limited to home and work. Another key feature of specialised sexualised violence services is holistic support for survivors of child sexual abuse and its long-term psychological and physical impact.

Some women’s centres provide support for women survivors of sexualised violence. However, this support is not always specialised and may therefore result in repeated referrals, as many survivors have unique needs, such as immediate forensic testing, complex trauma support and medical services, which general women’s centres supporting all survivors of VAW cannot necessarily provide. Services responding to survivors’ needs should ensure specific sexualised violence training and specialisation of service provision.

It is worth noting that different European countries have varied approaches to the provision of sexualised violence services. In some countries, women’s centres are offering specialised holistic support for all forms of VAW, including sexualised violence. The aim is to avoid multiple referrals and re-traumatisation, as well as ensure adequate and feminist support to survivors. Other countries have consolidated networks of rape crisis centres (RCCs), with trained staff offering immediate and long-term confidential survivor-led counselling and therapy and providing various services such as advocacy and prevention. For the first time, the questionnaire included two open questions about technology-facilitated violence against women and girls. One question inquired into the rise in such forms of violence, while the second assessed what strategies have been adopted by WSS to tackle such violence. This assessment is a starting point for the WAVE Network to gather a clearer picture of the needs and challenges across Europe and to guide future work to build the capacity of WSS to prevent and counter TFVAWG.

The questionnaire section on femicide was also reviewed to assess the status of data collection in each country and the state initiatives to prevent femicide, for instance, through systematic analysis of femicide (e.g., femicide reviews). The results are presented in a dedicated chapter that sheds light on the lack of harmonised definitions and data collection. At the end of the chapter, a table summarises some key findings: the number of reported femicide victims in each country, and additional details related to data collection.

text:
Section: Research preparation > Countries included in the data collection > Limitations of collected data

While all country delegates made efforts to ensure the data and information provided through the questionnaire were accurate, the figures presented should be interpreted with caution. In some cases, respondents were unable to obtain all relevant information and data. This was either due to limited capacity or because government agencies

either do not collect this data or do not make it available to the public; therefore, they could not present the complete picture of specialist services available in their country or detailed qualitative information in the different questionnaire sections. Due to this limitation, only limited comparisons with previous Country Reports are included in the analysis; instead, specific examples are used to showcase improvements or declines.

One limitation of the questionnaire concerns respondents' interpretations of the definitions, the types of services they reported, and how they classified them. Moreover, not all countries have the same systems in place to support survivors of VAW. While some models have been successfully implemented in certain countries, they may not be effective in other contexts, making the comparability of country situations difficult. This is the case with support services for survivors of sexualised violence, as mentioned in the previous section. To mitigate such differences, the respondents were provided with definitions embedded in each questionnaire section, and the WAVE Team held regular open online sessions and ad hoc meetings to clarify any doubts about the questionnaire.

text:
Section: Research preparation > Countries included in the data collection > Limitations of collected data

As mentioned above, although the report analyses 46 countries, five of them provided multiple questionnaires. This poses a challenge in data analysis and makes it more difficult to provide an accurate national overview. When presenting the data at the European level, information from different regions of the same country was combined, and internal differences were explained when relevant.

The tables in the report aim to summarise the results of the data collection, facilitate comparisons across countries, and provide an overview of the situation at the European level. When consulting the tables, footnotes should be considered, as the lack of data in some countries does not always allow for consistent comparisons across years or between data from different editions of the Country Report.

As emerged in previous reports, there are serious gaps in the availability and comparability of data concerning the recorded number of femicide victims in the 46 countries surveyed, as there is no Europe-wide data collection system or agreed use of the term femicide. These figures should be treated with caution. Data on the number of femicide victims were not available in nine of the countries surveyed, and the data available in the surveyed countries are not statistically robust and should be regarded as estimates based on the best available sources. The same applies to the number of survivors supported by WSS in 2024: in many cases, these numbers are estimates, while in others, no data were available. Therefore, the real number of survivors supported is likely much higher.

text:
Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > The foundation of survivor support

Women’s Specialist Services (WSS) are the cornerstone of Europe's response to violence against women and girls (VAWG). These services provide the first critical entry point for survivors seeking safety, support, and a path to reclaiming their lives. Unlike generic victim support services, WSS operate from a distinct rights-based, intersectional feminist approach. They are women-led, run by women for women, and fundamentally grounded in the principle of survivor agency, meaning women themselves determine the pace and direction of their recovery journey.

WSS adopt a gender-transformative methodology that distinguishes them from all other support structures. Their mission extends beyond individual support to address the societal systems that enable VAWG to persist. This dual mandate encompasses both prevention and response. Through primary prevention initiatives, WSS challenge gender stereotypes that devalue women and girls, promote bystander intervention when violence is witnessed, and deliver comprehensive sexuality education.

Through secondary prevention, the frontline response after violence occurs, WSS provide immediate, specialised support via helplines, shelters, rape crisis centres (RCCs), and women’s centres. These services create secure environments where all women can access compassionate, expert support and develop strategies to prevent and recover from violence, free from judgment or reprisal. This is why WSS are not only essential for crisis response but are also leaders in the primary prevention work this report identifies as critical to ending VAWG.

The expertise and approach that WSS bring cannot be replicated by generic services. Research consistently demonstrates that women experiencing sexual violence often withhold disclosure unless they perceive service providers as specialists who are open, knowledgeable, and trustworthy. Generic providers frequently lack this expertise, creating risks of disbelief, minimisation, or mishandling of disclosures that can cause women to withdraw from services entirely, leaving them unsupported and more vulnerable. WSS are trauma-informed, independent from state institutions, and possess a deep understanding of gendered violence dynamics that enables them to provide consistent, high-quality care tailored to each woman's specific circumstances and intersecting needs.

text:
Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > The threat of gender neutrality

Despite decades of evidence that gender-responsive specialist services are more effective than generic approaches in supporting survivors of VAWG, Europe faces a growing threat from gender-neutral policies. This shift has moved beyond far-right politics into mainstream discourse, making it more insidious.

Politically, gender neutrality serves to diminish the perceived impact of VAWG by claiming gender equality has been achieved. It falsely equates VAWG with violence against men, ignoring that approximately 90% of perpetrators of gender-based violence against women (GBVAW) are men, and women face disproportionate risks across every form of violence.

Gender neutrality also ignores that societal gender inequality persists across employment, leadership, pay equity, care responsibilities, political representation, and online violence. True progress requires equity, investing more in women’s rights and dismantling structures that undervalue women. We cannot reach equality by treating everyone identically when starting conditions are fundamentally unequal.

Economically, gender-neutral approaches are presented as cost-saving measures in times of austerity, allowing governments to consolidate services and reduce spending. This logic treats WSS as expendable, positioning generic victim support as adequate. It is not. Evidence shows that this apparent cost-saving is a false economy that will ultimately cost Europe far more.

Far from being a luxury, investing in WSS makes economic sense. Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > The economic case for investment

The reinstatement of the Global Gag Rule, USAID funding freeze, and US cuts to UN agencies have severely impacted gender equality and intersectional civil society organisations. Simultaneously, several European governments are diverting funds toward security and defence, further destabilising organisations that prevent and respond to VAWG.

This financial weakening is compounded by increased funding for anti-rights actors. Between 2019 and 2023, anti-gender organisations invested € 339.6 million<sup>52</sup> in lobbying to reverse progress on gender equality and women’s rights, ultimately aiming to undermine EU values of fundamental rights, democratic principles, and the rule of law. If Europe is serious about upholding fundamental rights and preventing VAWG, it must provide adequate, sustainable, long-term funding for WSS. A significant budget increase for programmes like CERV+ and its DAPHNE strand, exclusively dedicated to preventing and combating VAWG, sends a strong political message: protecting EU values, fundamental rights, and democracy is vital. This requires that funding reach frontline organisations, human rights defenders, and WSS directly.

<sup>52</sup> Neil Datta (2025) The Next Wave: How Religious Extremism Is Regaining Power, European Parliamentary Forum for Sexual and Reproductive Rights (EPF), https://www.epfweb.org/node/1147

text:
Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > Introduction

National women’s helplines are among the most vital and life-saving services for women and girls survivors of gender-based violence (GBV). They provide immediate access to confidential advice, emotional support, and information about rights and services. Women’s helplines in Europe emerged from the feminist movements of the 1970s and 1980s, simultaneously with the creation of women’s shelters and rape crisis centres (RCCs). In the United Kingdom, feminist activists established local women’s refuges and volunteer-run telephone lines where women could seek safety and advice. By the mid-1980s, these grassroots initiatives had grown into the first national helpline structures.<sup>53</sup>

Similar developments took place across Europe. In Austria, women’s organisations that had founded shelters in the late 1970s went on to set up hotlines that connected women across the country to immediate support.<sup>54</sup> In Germany, feminist groups created local helplines which were gradually consolidated into wider networks.<sup>55</sup> In the Nordic countries, helplines were established as part of the broader infrastructure of gender equality and welfare policies, often linked to women’s shelters or RCCs.

text:
Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > Introduction

In the Balkan region (former Yugoslavia), the first SOS helpline was founded in 1988 in Zagreb, Croatia, followed by the first SOS hotlines in Ljubljana, Slovenia, and in Belgrade, Serbia.<sup>56</sup> Soon, women’s helplines were opening across Europe. Decades before the Istanbul Convention was adopted and came into force, mandating State Parties that have ratified it to provide 24-hour hotlines for all forms of violence against women and girls (VAWG), women’s specialist services (WSS), NGOs, and feminist grassroots organisations and initiatives had already begun establishing these services.

These early helplines in Europe were deeply rooted in women’s self-organised activism. They reflected an understanding that women needed independent and safe spaces to speak freely about their experiences and to access practical, confidential, empathetic victim-centred support. Over time, many became professionalised and state-supported, but their feminist origins remain vitally important. They continue to remind us that helplines are not neutral specialised services, but part of a broader struggle for women’s human rights. But more than this, they represent a recognition that VAWG is not random or isolated, but a structural problem rooted in gender inequality.

text:
Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > Introduction

By contrast, where governments invest instead in generic or gender-neutral helplines, survivors are often left without the expertise and sensitivity they require. Gender-neutral services risk overlooking patterns of coercive control and may present violence as symmetrical between women and men. This can lead to inappropriate advice, unsafe referrals, and secondary victimisation. Moreover, in some political contexts, the promotion of gender-neutral services reflects a backlash against gender equality and a refusal to acknowledge VAWG as a structural problem requiring feminist solutions.

A national women’s helpline must therefore be specialist and comprehensive, covering all forms of violence against women (VAW). Women rarely experience violence in neatly separated categories, and the same survivor may be subjected to multiple forms of abuse, often simultaneously. A helpline that recognises this continuum of violence and responds from a gender-sensitive standpoint is better equipped to understand women’s experiences and provide meaningful assistance.

Specialist helplines are also essential because survivors frequently face disbelief, minimisation, or victim-blaming in broader society. A national women’s helpline, staffed by trained professionals or volunteers who believe survivors and understand the gendered dynamics of violence, offers the validation and solidarity that women need in order to seek support.

text:
Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > Introduction > International obligations

The Istanbul Convention (Article 24)<sup>57</sup> reflects this principle by requiring state-wide, 24/7, free helplines that address all forms of VAW. It emphasises that such services are not optional, but a legal obligation.

57 See Council of Europe, Istanbul Convention, Article 24.

58 See European Union, Directive (EU) 2024/1385, Article 27.

The Council of Europe Istanbul Convention sets out the minimum standards for national women’s helplines:

State-wide coverage
 24/7 availability
 Free of charge
 Confidential and anonymous
 Addressing all forms of VAW
 Providing services in relevant languages

These standards are echoed and reinforced by the EU Directive on Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence,<sup>58</sup> which requires that helplines are free, universally accessible, and inclusive of women with disabilities. The Directive specifies that multiple communication formats must be available, including national sign language and simplified language.

Both instruments also require adequate and sustainable state funding (Istanbul Convention Article 8, EU Directive Article 36). Without long-term investment, helplines cannot reliably function 24/7, train and retain staff, or expand accessibility. Funding through short-term projects or competitive tenders, while common, undermines the continuity and safety of services.

Section: Why women’s specialist services matter > Introduction > WAVE framework for data collection on national women’s helplines

The data presented in this chapter are based on WAVE’s 2025 data collection tool, which included a dedicated section on national women’s helplines. Respondents were asked to indicate whether a state-wide women’s helpline exists in their country, and to provide details about its operation, based on data from 2024. Specifically, questions covered:

The number of national women’s helplines and their names
 Which organisations run the helpline(s)
 Whether the helpline(s) is/are free of charge and available 24/7
 Whether multilingual support is provided, and if so, which languages are covered
 Which forms of VAW are addressed
 Main sources of funding (state, donations, international funding, or other)
 Call volumes in 2024, including total contacts and total individual callers, when available
 The three most common forms of violence reported
 Other helplines in the country (regional or specialised), including details on their scope and operation

This framework ensures consistent and comparable data collection across countries, and highlights both progress and remaining gaps in the provision of women’s helplines.

Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe

Table 7: Overview of service provision – national women’s helplines in Europe

Countries with at least one state-wide helpline

By 2024, 39 of 46 European countries (85%) report having at least one national women’s helpline supporting survivors of VAWG. The remaining 15% (seven countries) have some form of helpline provision at the national and/or regional level.

Seven countries<sup>59</sup> (15%) across Europe remain without a free, 24/7 national women’s helpline. In some cases, no statewide service exists at all, such as in Armenia and Belarus. In others, provision is fragmented or gender-neutral, as in Belgium, where separate helplines operate for Flemish- and French-speaking communities, none exclusively for women, and in Latvia, where helpline services exist, but those that are 24/7 are not specifically for survivors of VAW, and the one that is specialised does not operate 24/7.

Over half of European states continue to operate a single national women’s helpline, which is the model recommended by the Istanbul Convention. In 2024, 29 countries fall into this category. For women, this means one well-known number that can be called from anywhere in the country at any time.

responsibility under the Istanbul Convention. Yet the absence of proper provision in seven countries still leaves women without a guaranteed right to immediate, specialist, and accessible support.

Over half of European states continue to operate a single national women’s helpline, which is the model recommended by the Istanbul Convention. In 2024, 29 countries fall into this category. For women, this means one well-known number that can be called from anywhere in the country at any time.

A smaller group of countries reports two national helplines, such as in France, where the Violence Femmes Info line coexists with specialist lines on forced marriage and workplace harassment. In total, seven countries reported having two helplines.

In Türkiye, there are three main helplines providing support in cases of violence. The first is the national helpline, operated and financed by the Ministry of Family and Social Services. The hotline is free of charge and available 24/7, providing support in Turkish, Arabic, and Kurdish, open to various groups, but not specialised in supporting women survivors of violence. The two other helplines are the Emergency Hotline for Domestic Violence, run by the Federation of Women Associations of Türkiye, providing support to survivors of all forms of VAW, especially domestic violence, and Woman Support Line, run and funded by the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, providing support in Turkish, Kurdish, English and Arabic for all forms of VAW.

Spain has a national helpline and multiple regional helplines. The national helpline is called Service of attention to all forms of VAW, run by the Ministry of Equality, free of charge and available 24/7, offering multilingual support in Spanish, Catalan, Basque, Galician, English, French, German, Portuguese, Mandarin Chinese, Russian, Arabic, Romanian, Bulgarian, Tamazight and 39 other languages through a tele-translation service. It provides help for all forms of VAW and is funded by the state.

The data collected shows a high number of regional helplines in Serbia, with a total of nine licensed helplines listed. There is one national helpline and eight regional ones. This suggests that women are far more likely to rely on local or regional helplines run by women’s NGOs and shelters. For survivors, the reality is that multiple services may be essential to fill gaps left by the state.

◾ Seven countries operate two helplines

◾ Two countries operate three helplines

◾ The United Kingdom has four helplines, one for each of its nations

Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > National women’s helplines meeting Istanbul Convention standards > CASE STUDY: United Kingdom

Across the United Kingdom, all four nations, England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland, operate nation- al 24/7 domestic violence or VAW helplines, and each also has a separate, specialised sexual violence help- line or support line. This structure is relatively unique, as it ensures that in a comparatively small geographi- cal area, all jurisdictions maintain two fully functional, distinct helplines addressing different forms of VAWG.

England: The National Domestic Abuse Helpline (Ref- uge) offers 24/7, free, multilingual support to women affected by domestic violence. In addition, the Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line (Rape Crisis England & Wales) provides nationwide 24/7 support to anyone aged 16+ affected by sexual violence.

Wales: The Live Fear Free Helpline (Welsh Women’s Aid) offers 24/7, free, bilingual (Welsh/English) and multilingual support on all forms of VAW. Survivors of sexual violence in Wales can also access the Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line run by Rape Crisis England & Wales.

Scotland: Scotland’s Domestic Abuse and Forced Marriage Helpline (Scottish Women’s Aid) operates 24/7 and provides multilingual support. A separate Rape Crisis Scotland Helpline offers daily evening support to survivors of sexual violence.

Northern Ireland: The Domestic and Sexual Abuse Helpline (Nexus NI) is 24/7, free, and multilingual, offer- ing support to survivors of all genders. In addition, the Rowan Sexual Assault Referral Centre operates a ded- icated sexual violence helpline alongside forensic and medical services for survivors across Northern Ireland.

This dual-helpline model, with specialised servic- es for both domestic/VAW and sexual violence, is a distinguished feature of the United Kingdom context, demonstrating strong institutional recognition of the need for specialised, parallel response systems within each nation.

Most compliant helplines also ensure accessibility for di- verse groups of women by providing services in multiple languages. In some countries, this is delivered by multi- lingual staff, in others, through structured interpretation services. Increasingly, helplines are also expanding ac- cessibility by offering interpretation for deaf women and those with hearing difficulties, reflecting a commitment to inclusion.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention

While the overall picture shows evident progress, nine countries still lack a national women’s helpline that fully meets the requirements of the Istanbul Convention.

In the EU, seven states fall short due to limitations in their provision. In Belgium, there is no national women’s help- line due to structural and linguistic differences within the country. Instead, there are distinct helplines for each of the two major linguistic communities (Brussels-Wallonia and Flanders). In Latvia, there is no national helpline, but there are three other helplines supporting survivors of VAW. There is no specialised national women’s helpline in Mal- ta, but two generic helplines that can provide support also to women survivors of GBV. There is no national women’s helpline in the Netherlands, but there is a national helpline for domestic violence and child abuse, Safe Home, availa- ble 24/7 and free of charge, providing support to all survi- vors of violence as well as for professionals who want to report cases of child abuse and/or domestic violence.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention

Outside the EU, three additional countries remain non-com- pliant. In Armenia, 12 different helplines exist, most of them local or specialised, but no state-wide service is available, although there is a process underway to estab- lish a national helpline. The Ministry of Social Affairs runs a national helpline which is not specialised but can refer domestic violence cases to regional helplines, according to the location of the survivor. In Switzerland, discussions continue on establishing a national service, but provision remains limited to cantonal or regional levels, with the in- troduction of a national 24-hour helpline planned for May 2026. The only national women’s helpline in Belarus was the National Hotline for victims of family violence, which
was run by the international public association ‘Gender Perspectives’ from 2012 to 2021. As a result of state repressions against Belarusian civil society, ‘Gender Perspectives’ was compulsorily liquidated, and the helpline was indefinitely suspended in July 2021 when the office was raided by law enforcement. This situation has created significant challenges and limitations in accessing information on WSS in Belarus.

Taken together, these examples highlight the different ways in which gaps appear. In some contexts, helplines are under-resourced or restricted in scope, preventing them from offering the full level of accessibility required. In others, the absence of a state-wide women’s helpline reflects deeper structural or political barriers, including hostility to feminist organisations or the persistence of gender-neutral approaches that don’t take into account women’s specific experiences of violence.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Multilingual support

The Istanbul Convention emphasises that national women’s helplines should be accessible to all women, regardless of their language. This is particularly important for migrant and refugee women, many of whom face additional obstacles in seeking protection and support.

In 2024, 29 countries report that their national women’s helpline offers multilingual support. This represents the overwhelming majority of European states with helpline provision, showing that language accessibility has become a standard expectation. By contrast, five countries reported that their helplines are not multilingual, and in the remaining countries, information was not available. In North Macedonia, the national helpline offers support in Macedonian, Albanian, Roma and Turkish, although multilingual support is not available 24/7, but only when an operator who speaks one of these languages is on duty.

There are considerable examples of good practice. In Spain, the 016 helpline provides support in more than 50 languages through professional interpretation services, making it one of the most comprehensive models in Europe. The national helpline in Germany offers counselling in 18 languages, while in France, interpretation is available in more than 200 languages through a partnership for interpretation. In smaller states, multilingual services are often less available. In Slovenia, support is primarily available in Slovenian, English and neighbouring languages (Croatian and Bosnian), while in Denmark, two national women’s helplines provide multilingual support. One of them is the state-funded Live Without Violence’s National Hotline, providing multilingual support in any language provided by the interpretation service. The other one is Danner’s National Crisis Hotline, which operates in Danish and English.

Several countries also report efforts to make helplines more accessible for women with disabilities. In France, for

instance, the national helpline has developed video relay services and adapted online chat functions for deaf and hard-of-hearing women.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > CASE STUDY: Multilingual support in Germany’s national women’s helpline

The German national women’s helpline, the Violence against Women Helpline (Hilfetelefon ‘Gewalt gegen Frauen’), demonstrates how multilingual provision can be embedded into a national service. Operating 24/7 and free of charge, the helpline offers support in 18 languages through professional interpretation. This system enables migrant and refugee women to access specialist advice and support without language barriers, which is a crucial factor in ensuring equal access to protection.

In addition to spoken languages, the helpline has developed specific accessibility measures, including sign language support, Easy language and online chat, so that women with hearing impairments or communication difficulties can also reach the service. Germany’s model illustrates how national women’s helplines can extend their reach by integrating multilingual and inclusive communication as primary elements of service provision.

At the same time, the absence of multilingual provision in some countries leaves significant gaps. Women who do not speak the majority language may struggle to access vital information and support or may be unable to call the helplines entirely. This disproportionately affects migrant, refugee and minoritised women, who are often among the most vulnerable to violence.

Overall, the 2024 data confirms that multilingual accessibility is becoming the norm across Europe, but the quality and scope vary greatly. The strongest models are those that combine broad language provision with interpretation for women with disabilities, ensuring that all women can reach specialist feminist support when they need it.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Entities running national women’s helplines

The majority of national women’s helplines across Europe are run by women’s NGOs. This reflects the long history of feminist organisations in creating and sustaining these services, often decades before states assumed any responsibility. Examples include Austria, where the national helpline is operated by the Association of Autonomous Austrian Women’s Shelters, Croatia, where the Autonomous Women’s House Zagreb runs the line, and the Czech Republic, where the feminist organisation ROSA is now operating the European harmonised number for helplines for victims of VAW. In Hungary, the helpline is operated by NANE, while in Ireland, the national service is run by
NATIONAL WOMEN’S HELPLINES

Women’s Aid Ireland. These services are firmly rooted in a gendered understanding of VAW, which is central to their effectiveness.

In a smaller but still significant number of countries, national women’s helplines are operated directly by government ministries or state agencies. For example, in Greece, by the General Secretariat for Gender Equality; in Germany, by the Federal Office for Family and Civil Society Tasks; and in Georgia, by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In Türkiye, three parallel helplines operate, one of which, ALO 183, is managed by the Ministry of Family and Social Services.

There are also mixed models, where responsibility is shared between state institutions and NGOs, or where contracts have shifted between providers. In Finland, the helpline is run by the Institute of Health and Welfare in partnership with NGOs.

Despite the differences in who runs them, the crucial factor is whether helplines operate from a gendered perspective and ensure feminist, survivor-centred support. Where women’s NGOs remain at the centre of service provision, helplines are most clearly grounded in this expertise.

In some countries, more than one national women’s helpline operates in parallel. While the state may fund or manage the official line, additional services are frequently run by women’s NGOs. These often have a more specialised focus, reflecting the diverse needs of survivors. For example, in Bosnia & Herzegovina, Medica Zenica operates a state-wide helpline for survivors of war-related sexual violence. In Denmark, the feminist organisation Danner runs a national service, operated by volunteers, alongside the general helpline. In Finland, the Women’s Line (Naisten Linja) provides a feminist helpline complementing the state’s service through the Institute for Health and Welfare. In Albania, the NGO Psycho-Social Center Vatra operates an additional helpline, while in Croatia, Women’s Help Now provides another women’s helpline for survivors of VAW.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Funding for national women’s helplines

The Istanbul Convention and the EU Directive on VAW and domestic violence both make clear that governments have the responsibility to ensure adequate and sustainable funding for women’s specialist support services, including national helplines and that they should not have to rely on insecure resources such as donations or short-term international projects.

In 2024, the majority of national women’s helplines across Europe reported receiving at least some state funding. This represents substantial progress in recognising helplines as part of the state’s core duty to protect women’s rights. However, five countries still lack state funding for their national helplines: Bosnia & Herzegovina, Hungary, Poland, Russia, and Slovakia. Additionally, in Serbia, two of the nine helplines receive state funding, while the others

rely on donations and international financing. In these contexts, women’s NGOs continue to provide services with limited or no public support, often at significant cost to their sustainability.

Alongside state support, 17 countries report that their national helplines depend at least partly on donations from foundations, trusts, or individuals. While donations can indeed supplement resources, relying on them to cover core costs undermines the principle that specialist services are a state obligation.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Funding for national women’s helplines

International funding continues to play a crucial role. Fourteen countries report dependence on international donors and projects, including Albania, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Croatia, Hungary, Georgia, Moldova, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Slovakia, Türkiye, and Ukraine. In these contexts, helplines are often sustained by EU projects or international humanitarian aid, rather than secure state budgets.

In Russia, the highly complex and threatening environment severely limits communication among women’s NGOs. It is often impossible to verify how organisations operate or what strategies they employ. Information on funding sources is particularly sensitive for security reasons and therefore cannot be publicly disclosed. In the case of the POLINA Centre, while efforts are made to diversify funding, the organisation’s main sources of support for many years have been international donors and private contributions.

In Bosnia & Herzegovina, NGOs in the Federation continue to operate SOS lines on a volunteer basis with no state financing, despite new legislation recognising women’s right to helpline support. In Hungary, both NANE and PATENT depend on international grants and private donations, with much of the work carried out by volunteers. In the Netherlands, the government funds a generic, gender-neutral helpline (Safe Home), while feminist NGOs continue to campaign for an independent women’s helpline that meets Istanbul Convention standards. In Serbia, only two out of nine national helplines receive state support, while the rest rely on international projects and donations. In Switzerland, no state-wide helpline exists, and provision is left to individual cantons, where services are volunteer-based. These examples demonstrate that while state funding has increased since 2023, it is still not adequate, secure and sustainable.

In the Netherlands, the government funds a generic, gender-neutral helpline (Safe Home), while feminist NGOs continue to campaign for an independent women’s helpline that meets Istanbul Convention standards. In Serbia, only two out of nine national helplines receive state support, while the rest rely on international projects and donations. In Switzerland, no state-wide helpline exists, and provision is left to individual cantons, where services are volunteer-based. These examples demonstrate that while state funding has increased since 2023, it is still not adequate, secure and sustainable.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Information on the number of calls

Across Europe, national women’s helplines received hundreds of thousands of calls in 2024; 32 countries were able to provide either exact numbers or estimates of the number of calls, and helplines in these countries received over 900,000 calls. The highest numbers were reported in larger states such as Spain, where the national helpline received nearly 59,000 calls, and France, where the state line recorded over 152,000 calls. Smaller states also show
significant demand: in Austria, 5,425 calls were recorded, while in Finland, the Nollalinja registered over 15,000 calls. In Hungary, the combined number of calls for the two helplines run by NANE and PATENT is over 25,000. A total of 48,369 calls were answered by Sweden’s Kvinnofridslinjen's staff in 2024.

text:

The number of calls to the helplines is also substantial in non-EU states. In England, the national helpline run by Women’s Aid reported over 135,000 callers. In Armenia, while there is no single state-wide helpline, twelve regional helplines together handled 3,877 calls, with most linked to domestic violence. In Albania, the national helpline for women and girls received 4,658 calls, a 12% increase compared to the previous year, indicating a growing trust in the support system available to survivors of VAWG. Montenegro received 2,114, and North Macedonia 760 calls.

It is important to note that statistics are not directly comparable across states. Some helplines count total contacts, including repeat calls, while others record only the number of individual callers. Some also provide support through chat. The extent of public awareness of the helpline, its visibility in national campaigns, and levels of state support also shape the number of calls received. Nevertheless, the overall picture confirms that women’s helplines are among the most widely accessed specialist support services in Europe.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Most common forms of violence reported

When asked about the three most common forms of violence reported, the majority of helplines identified domestic violence as the most common. Where domestic violence was not reported as the most common was in the countries that did not have general data on the calls. Information was also collected for different types of violence that occur within domestic violence. In about two-thirds of the countries, psychological and physical violence were also reported among the three most common, while sexualised violence was included in the three most common in 11 countries. Economic violence was among the most prevalent in seven countries, while stalking was mentioned only in the Czech Republic. Violence directly or indirectly affecting children was reported as one of the most common forms of violence in the Czech Republic, Azerbaijan, Estonia, the Netherlands and Cyprus.

Other frequently reported issues included child abuse and child protection concerns, often linked to family violence, followed by cases of sexual abuse and assault, as well as reports of human trafficking and exploitation. In Moldova, the most commonly reported form of violence was physical, often occurring in combination with other types, accounting for 65% of all cases. This is followed by psychological violence (22%), economic violence (7%), and sexual violence (4%). These figures highlight that many survivors face multiple, overlapping forms of abuse, with physical violence being the most prevalent among those who sought help.

It is worth noting that domestic violence means all acts of physical, sexual, coercive, psychological, or economic violence and that different forms of VAWG intersect. For example, in Hungary, most callers reach out to NANE due to domestic violence, which typically includes a combination of verbal, psychological, economic, and physical abuse and in many cases, sexual violence as well. A significant proportion of these situations also involves children. Most women contacting the PATENT helpline seek legal guidance on divorce proceedings resulting from domestic violence and matters of child custody.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Other national helplines in Europe

In many countries, additional helplines exist together with or instead of the official national line. These may be regional, local, or dedicated to particular forms of VAWG or GBV. They play a vital role in reaching survivors who might not otherwise access support.

In England, for example, 181 local domestic abuse services run helplines. They are mostly for local residents and callers to receive support over the phone, sometimes before accessing other support services. Other national helpline services for other forms of VAWG include Modern Slavery Helpline, Revenge Porn Helpline, and Honour-Based Abuse Helpline. Similarly, in Croatia, around 20 separate helplines exist, many operated by women’s organisations that specialise in areas such as sexual violence, human trafficking, and domestic violence. In Estonia, there are 16 regional helplines run by women’s support centres and operating 24/7. In addition, the organisation Lifeline runs a specific helpline for survivors of human trafficking and sexual exploitation, available during limited hours.

text:
Section: Findings on the situation of national women’s helplines in Europe > Helplines that are not yet compliant with the Istanbul Convention > Other national helplines in Europe

Specialised helplines also respond to specific forms of violence. In Austria, women have access to helplines focused on sexual violence, while in Greece, there is a helpline for supporting survivors of trafficking in persons, offering multilingual support in over 200 languages through tele-interpretation, and available 24/7. In Bosnia & Herzegovina (Federation), the organisation Medica Zenica runs a unique helpline for survivors of war-related sexual violence and their families, which is free of charge and available 24/7. In France, there is the Family Planning hotline, a reference centre for issues related to contraception, abortion, sexually transmitted infections, violence and sexuality, as well as a helpline for advocacy against discrimination towards women with disabilities.

In some countries, there are parallel helplines that reflect different institutional approaches. In Denmark, several helplines operate in addition to the national one, including targeted support for children and youth exposed to domestic or dating violence, medical and psychological support after rape/assault, therapeutic support for families affected by violence, general support for victims of violent crime, specialised support for stalking and others.
NATIONAL WOMEN’S HELPLINES

In some European countries, the only state-wide helpline available is a gender-neutral service. These helplines respond to all survivors of domestic violence or child abuse, and sometimes to broader issues of violence or social welfare. While they provide an important point of contact, they do not meet the Istanbul Convention’s requirement for specialist helplines for survivors of all forms of VAWG.

One example is the Netherlands, where the government funds Safe Home (Veilig Thuis), a 24/7 service covering domestic violence and child abuse. Although it is widely accessible and free of charge, the helpline operates from a gender-neutral framework. Women’s NGOs in the country continue to campaign for an independent women’s helpline, grounded in a gendered understanding of violence against women.

text:
Section: Conclusion

The latest findings on national women’s helplines in Europe show both important progress and persistent gaps. Thirty-nine out of 46 countries now have at least one national women’s helpline, and 37 of these meet the minimum standards set out in the Istanbul Convention by being free of charge, available 24/7, and operating from a gendered understanding of VAW.

Helplines continue to play a crucial role as an entry point for women into protection and support. They provide confidential, immediate assistance, often serving as the first contact for women survivors of VAWG. They are also the key point of contact, referring women survivors to other essential specialised services and institutions. They are also accessible to women who might otherwise be isolated, including those in rural or remote areas. The increase in provision of multilingual services further strengthens accessibility for diverse groups of women, including migrants and refugees, and highlights the principle of non-discrimination in service provision.

Despite this progress, significant challenges remain. Some countries still lack a fully compliant national women’s helpline, and in others, provision is limited to only certain forms of violence, such as domestic violence, or they are delivered through gender-neutral services. Funding also continues to be a concern, with many helplines reliant on short-term projects, donations, or international grants rather than secure and sustainable state support. This instability undermines both the continuity of services and states’ obligations under international standards.

Across Europe, women’s helplines receive nearly a million calls each year, most commonly concerning domestic, physical, and psychological violence, but also sexualised, economic, and technology-facilitated violence. Each call is a vital step in breaking isolation and seeking safety, confirming the indispensable role of helplines in comprehensive systems of protection.

text:
Section: Recommendations

Each European country must establish at least one national women’s helpline providing specialist, gender-specific support on all forms of VAWG, operating 24/7, free of charge, and grounded in feminist, survivor-centred principles.

States must guarantee adequate, secure, and long-term public funding for national women’s helplines, avoiding reliance on volunteers or private donations. Public funding should prioritise women’s NGOs with demonstrated expertise, while allowing them to access complementary international or philanthropic resources without reducing state obligations.

National women’s helplines should be equipped to provide referrals to other relevant services, including WSS. Governments must strengthen co operation frameworks to ensure smooth referral pathways and coordinated support across sectors.

States should develop standardised data collection and reporting practices for national women’s helplines, in consultation with WSS, in order to better understand the scope of VAWG, track helpline effectiveness, and improve service provision.

National women’s helplines must ensure that all survivors can access support by ensuring the availability of multilingual services, when possible, by staff with lived knowledge of the challenges and barriers experienced by migrant and refugee women. Accessibility of helplines can be improved with the use of technology, e.g., including chat options, mobile apps, and integration into social media platforms for wider reach.

States should guarantee nationwide visibility of helpline information, ensuring that the national helpline number is widely promoted across the country, including in media coverage related to VAWG.

States must recognise the specific contribution of WSS in providing helpline services and refrain from replacing or prioritising gender-neutral helplines over women’s specialist helplines, as they risk depriving survivors of a gender-specific service.

Helpline staff must receive comprehensive training informed by a gender-specific understanding of VAWG, including knowledge of legal rights, regional contexts, and all relevant provisions for women survivors of violence. The different needs of diverse groups of women need to be addressed by helpline staff in collaboration with specialised women’s organisations catering to specific groups.

text:
Section: Recommendations > Introduction

Shelter is one of the most fundamental components of a comprehensive response to violence against women (VAW). For women whose homes have become places of fear, control, and physical danger, access to secure accommodation can mean the difference between life and death. Shelters are not merely emergency spaces but essential specialist support services that uphold women’s human rights, autonomy, and dignity. They enable survivors of violence to escape abuse, recover from trauma, and rebuild their lives in safety and independence.

The term ‘women-only shelters’ refers to shelters exclusively for women survivors of violence and their children (if any), and ensures immediate access to safe accommodation. These provide empowering support based on a feminist and gender-specific approach, focusing on the human rights and safety of survivors. The functions of women’s shelters go beyond providing a safe place to stay in an emergency. Shelters also offer long-term support in order to provide women and their children with the opportunity and resources necessary to resume their lives free from violence. Some examples of services provided by women-only shelters include: counselling, legal advice and assistance throughout legal proceedings, support to enter/re-enter the labour market, and move-on support to find long-term accommodation after staying in the women’s shelter.

text:
Section: Recommendations > Introduction

Besides women-only shelters, accommodation for women survivors of VAW can also be provided by other shelters. Shelters included under this category do not have to be specialised or gender-specific, but they should still provide some level of support to all survivors of violence, such as women, men, and people who identify as LGBTIQ+. Shelters under this category also include services that provide temporary housing and general shelters.

The European women’s shelter movement has its roots in feminist activism of the 1970s, when women across Europe and beyond organised collectively to challenge male VAW that was normalised and hidden within the family. The first shelters were founded by women for women as grassroots initiatives born out of solidarity and political consciousness. Feminists who founded the first shelters were also the first ones to recognise and claim that VAW was not a private problem but a structural manifestation of gender inequality. These early shelters were often established with no state support and against prevailing social and political norms that denied the existence of violence within the home. They were spaces of resistance, providing physical safety alongside awareness-raising, collective empowerment, and advocacy for legal and social change. Their feminist approach was revolutionary in its insistence that intimate partner violence was rooted in unequal power relations and must be addressed as a matter of justice and human rights.

text:
Section: Recommendations > Introduction

Over time, these pioneering efforts evolved into national networks and international alliances, among which the WAVE Network plays a leading role. WAVE and its members uphold the legacy of the feminist shelter movement, defending the rights of women survivors, promoting high-quality, women-centred services, and challenging trends that undermine the gendered understanding of violence.

Shelters have thus been both practical responses to violence and engines of systemic change. They have exposed the pervasiveness of male violence, influenced public awareness, shaped national and international policies, and contributed to the recognition of VAW as a human rights violation.

The Istanbul Convention and WAVE’s standards define what constitutes an adequate and rights-based shelter service. A shelter must provide more than a bed: it must ensure physical safety, confidentiality, comprehensive support, and empowerment.

At a minimum, shelters should:

Be accessible to all women, including those with disabilities, migrant women, or those from rural areas, who may face additional barriers or discrimination in accessing support services.

Be accessible 24/7 and located throughout the country, including in rural areas.

text:
Section: Recommendations > Introduction

Be secure and confidential, with clear safety and protection protocols.

Employ trained female staff with expertise in VAW.

Provide individualised needs assessments, risk management, and safety planning.

Offer counselling, advocacy, legal and psychological support, and assistance in accessing justice, health care, social protection, and housing.

Support economic empowerment and long-term reintegration through employment and education initiatives.

Be free of charge for women without means.

And operate on the basis of women’s empowerment, non-victimisation, and self-determination.
WOMEN’S SHELTERS

Shelters should also guarantee child-friendly environments and employ trained childcare workers to support children’s recovery.

Quantitative standards are equally important for ensuring that the number of shelter beds matches the population and its needs. In its Explanatory Report, the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (Istanbul Convention), recommends one shelter place per 10,000 inhabitants.<sup>60</sup> In WAVE’s methodology, one family place equals one bed space.

text:
Section: Recommendations > Introduction

While this standard represents a minimum benchmark, experience across Europe shows that real demand often exceeds these numbers, particularly in times of economic crisis, conflict, or social disruption. Sustainable funding, geographic coverage, and high-quality standards are just as significant as meeting the required number of shelter places. In addition to ensuring an adequate number of shelter places, many countries also highlight the importance of removing perpetrators from the home so that women and children do not have to relocate. Depending on the national context, some systems prioritise expanding shelter capacity, while others emphasise perpetrator removal measures, thereby reducing overall demand for shelter accommodation.

Women-only shelters embody the feminist principles that shaped the movement and ensure services are grounded in a gendered understanding of violence. Women-only environments are vital for survivors’ safety and healing. Many women have experienced violence from men, including intimate partners, relatives, traffickers, or others. The presence of men in shelters can re-trigger trauma, reinforce fear, and undermine women’s sense of security. In women-only spaces, survivors can rebuild trust, regain autonomy, and experience solidarity with other women.

Evidence across Europe demonstrates that women-only, feminist-led shelters provide higher-quality, more holistic, and longer-term support. Their methodologies prioritise empowerment, self-determination, and rights-based advocacy. They also act as critical advocates for systemic change, contributing to policy reforms and awareness-raising about gender-based violence (GBV).

In women-only spaces, survivors can rebuild trust, regain autonomy, and experience solidarity with other women.

Evidence across Europe demonstrates that women-only, feminist-led shelters provide higher-quality, more holistic, and longer-term support. Their methodologies prioritise empowerment, self-determination, and rights-based advocacy. They also act as critical advocates for systemic change, contributing to policy reforms and awareness-raising about gender-based violence (GBV).

text:
Section: Recommendations > PRINCIPLES OF A WOMEN’S SHELTER

According to Away from Violence – Guidelines for Setting Up and Running a Women’s Refuge (WAVE, 2004),<sup>61</sup> a women’s shelter (or women’s refuge) provides safe accommodation for women and their children who have experienced domestic violence, enabling them to live without fear of further abuse. Its primary purpose is safety, but its role extends far beyond providing a temporary place to stay.

Grounded in a feminist and human rights–based approach, a shelter is guided by the principles of women’s empowerment, solidarity, and advocacy for women’s rights. The central aim is to help women overcome the powerlessness created by violence, regain self-esteem, and rebuild the capacity for a self-determined and independent life.

Shelters provide crisis intervention and ongoing support, including counselling, legal and practical assistance, housing and employment advice, and help throughout legal procedures. Support must be offered by trained female counsellors who understand the gendered dynamics of violence and believe women’s stories without prejudice. Women are seen as experts in their own situations, and counselling focuses on empowerment rather than pathology.

text:
Section: Recommendations > PRINCIPLES OF A WOMEN’S SHELTER

Shelters are also communal spaces, offering an environment where women and children can experience new, non-violent ways of living and relating. They serve as models of equality and shared responsibility, helping women overcome internalised gender stereotypes and rediscover their strength and agency.

Beyond their direct support role, women’s shelters fulfil an essential public and political function. They raise awareness about domestic violence, challenge social norms that perpetuate male violence, cooperate with professionals and institutions, and engage in prevention, education, and advocacy. They act as agents of social change, exposing the structural and political roots of male violence and demanding accountability from perpetrators and society.

Fundamentally, shelters are built on the principles of:

Safety – secure, confidential, and protective accommodation

Empowerment – supporting women to regain control over their lives

60 See Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (Istanbul Convention): Explanatory Report, para. 135.

61 See WAVE Network (2004) Away from Violence – Guidelines for Setting Up and Running a Women’s Refuge.
 Solidarity and advocacy – believing survivors and standing beside them without neutrality toward violence
 Feminist understanding – recognising violence as rooted in gender inequality and power imbalances
 Collectivity – creating a supportive community that models equality and cooperation
 Social responsibility – raising public awareness, influencing policy, and preventing violence

Only services that fulfil these functions, ensuring safety, empowerment, advocacy, feminist values, and societal engagement, can rightly be called a women’s shelter.

However, the trend toward gender-neutral service models threatens these achievements. Increasingly, public authorities allocate funding through competitive procurement that prioritises cost-efficiency over expertise. Generic or commercial providers often lack the gendered understanding necessary to support survivors effectively. As a result, feminist NGOs are losing funding or being excluded from public contracts, leading to a loss of specialised knowledge, continuity, and trust from survivors.

Maintaining women-only shelters is therefore not merely a question of service design, but a matter of human rights, equality, and feminist principles. They represent both a safe haven and a political commitment to ending male VAW.

text:
Section: Recommendations > International obligations

States have binding obligations under international and regional human rights instruments to establish and maintain adequate shelter services for women survivors of violence. The Istanbul Convention, in Article 23, requires that:

> “Parties shall take the necessary legislative or other measures to provide for the setting-up of appropriate, easily accessible shelters in sufficient numbers to provide safe accommodation for and to reach out proactively to victims, especially women and their children”.<sup>62</sup>

To support the implementation of Article 23, the Council of Europe published its Quality Guidelines for Shelters for Victims of Violence against Women and Domestic Violence

in 2021.<sup>63</sup> These Guidelines specify that shelter systems should be independent, women-led, and non-profit, and that the safety and autonomy of survivors must be the guiding principles of all operations. Services should be comprehensive, encompassing immediate protection, psychological and legal support, advocacy, and assistance in securing long-term housing and economic stability. Staff should be trained women professionals with expertise in GBV, trauma, and intersectional approaches. States must ensure sustainable, long-term funding rather than project-based or competitive procurement systems to guarantee continuity and prevent the erosion of women’s specialist services (WSS). The Guidelines also emphasise that all women must be able to access shelters, including migrant and refugee women, women with disabilities, older women, and those without residence status or financial resources.

Section: Recommendations > International obligations

The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) imposes obligations on States Parties to eliminate discrimination and ensure women’s right to live free from violence.<sup>64</sup> General Recommendation No. 35 (2017)<sup>65</sup> affirmed that States Parties must exercise due diligence to prevent, investigate, punish, and provide reparation for acts of VAW, including by ensuring access to safe shelters and support services.

Within the European Union (EU), several legal and policy instruments reinforce these obligations. The EU Gender Equality Strategy 2020–2025 prioritises the eradication of GBV and the strengthening of WSS.<sup>66</sup> The EU Victims’ Rights Directive (2012/29/EU)<sup>67</sup> already requires that all victims of crime have access to confidential, free-of-charge support, but it does not explicitly guarantee specialised women-only services.

Section: Recommendations > International obligations

In 2024, the EU Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence obliges Member States to ensure the availability of shelters and interim accommodations to all survivors of violence. It requires that services shall be provided in sufficient numbers, be easily accessible and can accommodate the specific needs of women, including by providing women-only shelters with room for children.<sup>68</sup>

While the Preamble to EU Directive 2024/1385 (paragraphs 58–59) recognises women’s specialist support services as providing tailored, integrated assistance to survivors, it problematically frames them as optional supplements to general victim support rather than as essential, autonomous components. Crucially, the Preamble lacks the

text:
Section: Recommendations > International obligations > Findings on the situation of women-only shelters in Europe

Data collected for the WAVE Country Report 2025 from 46 European countries show that there are 3,224 shelters accessible to women, of which 2,365 are women-only shelters. Altogether, these shelters provide approximately 48,860 bed spaces for a total population of more than 847 million people. This remains far below the Istanbul Convention’s minimum standard of one family place per 10,000 inhabitants, requiring an estimated 84,732 bed spaces across Europe. Only 12 countries currently meet this standard, as well as Northern Ireland, as separate data was collected for the four United Kingdom entities.

Within the 27 EU Member States, there are 2,371 shelters accessible to women, including 1,737 women-only shelters, offering 33,450 bed spaces. This represents a 40% shortage in provision, with nine EU Member States meeting the Istanbul Convention benchmark. In non-EU European countries (19 in total), there are 853 shelters accessible to women, including 628 women-only shelters, providing 15,410 bed spaces. The gap is even more severe, with 62% of the required beds missing, and only four countries meeting the Istanbul Convention standard.

text:
Section: Recommendations > International obligations > COUNTRY EXAMPLE: Republic of Moldova

In 2024, the Republic of Moldova reported 13 women-only shelters providing 235 bed spaces for women and their children, a significant increase from eight shelters and 181 beds in 2022. With this expansion, Moldova now nearly meets the Istanbul Convention’s minimum standard, with only seven beds (3%) still missing. Shelters operate across most regions, though coverage remains uneven, with rural and remote areas still lacking adequate access to services.

Shelters are operated by a mix of public authorities, NGOs, religious organisations, and national institutions, reflecting a hybrid model of service provision. Local public authorities manage the majority of shelters under the coordination of the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, while a smaller number are run by non-governmental organisations. Among them, Casa Mărioarei remains the only feminist-run shelter in the country, offering a comprehensive, empowerment-based approach grounded in women’s rights and survivor-centred support.

Funding for women’s shelters primarily comes from state and local budgets, complemented by international donors and occasional religious or private contributions. Despite progress in expanding capacity, challenges persist, particularly in ensuring stable funding, retaining qualified staff, and meeting the needs of women with disabilities or from rural areas. Overall, Moldova’s shelter system demonstrates significant growth and institutionalisation, yet continued investment and stronger coordination with feminist NGOs are essential to ensure full compliance with international standards.

text:
Section: Accessibility of women’s shelters > → 24/7 accessibility

Data collected for the WAVE Country Report 2025 show that women-only shelters are accessible around the clock in most European countries. In total, 67% of countries (31 out of 46) report that all or most women-only shelters offer 24/7 access, ensuring immediate availability for women escaping violence at any time. However, in 22% (10 countries), only some shelters provide 24/7 access, and two countries (4%), Belarus and Greece, report no round-the-clock access. In three countries, the situation remains unknown or unclear, often due to fragmented data or decentralised service provision.

This unevenness highlights a continued geographical and policy gap: while some states maintain comprehensive access, others restrict entry to office hours or rely on referral mechanisms that delay safety and protection.

Comments from the WAVE delegates who provided the data further reveal that 24/7 access often depends on interpretation and capacity. In several countries, such as Finland and the Netherlands, all shelters or emergency crisis centres provide full 24-hour access, ensuring immediate admission at any time. In others, including Belgium (Flanders) and Iceland, 24/7 accessibility refers primarily to the availability of hotlines or on-call staff, rather than guaranteed physical admission.

In countries like Luxembourg, North Macedonia, and Poland, shelters are reachable at night only through police or emergency referrals, which can create delays or exclude women who seek help independently. Some comments also noted that funding limitations or local administrative rules restrict night-time intake. In Romania, several categories of shelters exist, differentiated by the range of services provided and the duration of accommodation. Emergency reception centres offer immediate, short-term refuge for women survivors of violence. These centres are accessible 24/7 and typically accommodate women for a period of two to six months, providing essential services such as food, basic medical care, and psychological support. Recovery centres, on the other hand, provide a more stable and supportive environment with comprehensive assistance, including social services, legal counselling, and rehabilitation programmes. Their primary aim is to support women in regaining autonomy and rebuilding their lives free from violence, with stays lasting up to one year or longer, depending on individual needs.

text:
Section: Accessibility of women’s shelters > → Women’s shelters accessible free of charge

Across Europe, most women-only shelters continue to provide free accommodation and services, ensuring that survivors can access safety without financial barriers. However, the latest data show that 11 out of 46 countries (24%) report that women may be expected to contribute

financially for their stay. These countries are: Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Slovakia, Slovenia, and parts of the United Kingdom (Scotland and Wales).

In Belgium and the Netherlands, payment is systematically required, structured as a regulated co-payment model linked to income or social welfare rules. In both contexts, women are routinely expected to contribute a proportion of their accommodation costs, often calculated in accordance with municipal or social housing regulations. In the Netherlands, these costs are usually paid for through social welfare or benefits, which the women’s shelters help women apply for with the municipalities. Women who already have income from a salary or otherwise pay from this income. In no case are accommodation costs a barrier to accessing women’s shelters. In Brussels and Wallonia, women are expected to pay for their accommodation in the shelter, meaning undocumented women without sufficient income have limited access to women-only shelters, whereas in Flanders, accommodation is free for the first 12 weeks of a stay in a shelter with a secret address. After this twelve-week period, women are expected to cover the accommodation costs either through their own means or through a contribution from the Public Centre for Social Welfare.

Women who already have income from a salary or otherwise pay from this income. In no case are accommodation costs a barrier to accessing women’s shelters. In Brussels and Wallonia, women are expected to pay for their accommodation in the shelter, meaning undocumented women without sufficient income have limited access to women-only shelters, whereas in Flanders, accommodation is free for the first 12 weeks of a stay in a shelter with a secret address. After this twelve-week period, women are expected to cover the accommodation costs either through their own means or through a contribution from the Public Centre for Social Welfare.

text:
Section: Accessibility of women’s shelters > → Women’s shelters accessible free of charge

In the remaining countries, payment is conditional or occasional. Women may be asked to contribute only if they have an income or receive social welfare benefits, while those without financial means are accommodated free of charge. In Germany, for instance, co-payment practices vary regionally depending on local funding arrangements. In France, it is based on the woman's income. In Ireland, women are expected to pay from approximately € 30–€ 60 per week, but the inability to pay is commonly considered by services. In Denmark and Luxembourg, shelters may apply small daily or weekly fees for women with income, which are waived in hardship cases. In Slovenia, shelters charge women 30% of the financial social assistance, but this can be adjusted according to income, whereas in Slovakia, accommodation is either free for the first few months or subject to only symbolic payments. Any contributions required later are typically adjusted based on the woman’s individual financial situation, including her income and essential expenses. In the Czech Republic, women are also expected to pay a fee for their stay. In Wales, he majority of the cost is met by Housing Benefit, but survivors also pay a minimal weekly service charge. In Scotland, women are expected to pay for their accommodation in shelters, but most do so through housing benefits.

By contrast, the majority of countries, 35 out of 46 (76%), confirm that shelter services are entirely free of charge. In Russia, church-affiliated shelters may ask women to help with domestic chores or community work, but no monetary payment is requested.
